title: Shared Roots: Abraham, Moses, and the Prophets You Both Honor
summary: How much of the Bible's cast of prophets Islam also honors, and why that shared foundation is a good place to start this collection.

body.text: If you grew up Christian, one of the most disorienting parts of learning about Islam can be discovering how much is genuinely shared before you even get to the real differences. This collection is built to help you understand and explain your journey to Christian family and friends, not to win an argument with them — so it starts with common ground, not disagreement.
The same prophets, honored in both faiths

Adam, Noah (Nuh), Abraham (Ibrahim), Isaac (Ishaq), Jacob (Ya'qub), Joseph (Yusuf), Moses (Musa), David (Dawud), Solomon (Sulayman), and Jesus (Isa) — all of these figures from the Bible appear in the Quran too, honored as prophets sent by the same God. Islam doesn't treat itself as an unrelated new religion; it presents itself as the continuation of the same prophetic line Christians and Jews already recognise, correcting what Islam holds to be later distortions rather than replacing the whole story.
Abraham specifically: a shared father figure

Abraham holds a uniquely central place in both traditions — Christians, Jews, and Muslims are all sometimes called "Abrahamic faiths" for exactly this reason. The Quran describes Ibrahim as a model of sincere monotheism and submission to God (the literal meaning of "Islam"), and Muslims trace the practice of Hajj to rites connected to Ibrahim and his family. Recognising this shared reference point can make conversations with Christian family feel less like starting from zero.

body.translation: Say, We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants, and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and we submit to Him.

body.text: Where the shared story starts to diverge

This lesson is deliberately about what's shared — the real theological differences (the nature of Jesus, the Trinity, the crucifixion, and more) are covered honestly in the lessons that follow this collection. Naming the common ground first isn't about softening those differences; it's about giving you an accurate starting point, since most Christian family members will already recognise these names, even if they've never heard how Islam describes them.

body.question: If Islam shares so many prophets with Christianity, why do Muslims and Christians disagree so much?
body.answer: The shared prophets are a real, genuine overlap — but Islam and Christianity describe some of these figures, and especially Jesus, quite differently, and Islam holds a different view of what these prophets' followers should believe and do today. Shared characters don't mean an identical story; the next lessons in this collection get into exactly where and why the accounts diverge.

body.question: Is it fair to call Islam an "Abrahamic religion" like Christianity and Judaism?
body.answer: Yes — this is standard terminology used by scholars of religion generally, not just by Muslims, precisely because all three trace their core religious identity back through Abraham and share significant scriptural overlap, even while differing sharply on theology and practice.
